title: Banjo players, Billy Eastwood and Snoozer Quinn with Whiteman
summary: Billy Eastwood's banjo tuning argument with Pinkerton, Whiteman's laughter, and Snoozer Quinn meeting Whiteman backstage and his time on tour.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about who some of your favorite banjo players were back in those times.

Well, I liked Jules. He was fine. And Billy Eastwood was very good. Billy tuned his banjo. Now, Billy could play both tunings. But Billy tuned his banjo ukulele styling. And that's why he and Pinkertour had quite an argument one time. And so Pinkertour says, all right, all right. He put up a piece of music. He says, for instance, he says, now with that tuning you can't play this piece. He says, here's a piece. Play this piece. And he put it up there and Billy took the piece and he just took his banjo and played it right off. He could read, see.

And that was so astounding that I have never seen Paul Whiteman's stomach shake so, you know, all my life. A laugh. You know, if you could get anything on anybody, old Pops would, he'd stand back there and he'd really give you a big belly laugh, in other words. He had the equipment. Oh, he had the equipment. And he'd really, he'd really, he was a wonderful person. And like when Snoozer Quinn, he came backstage at St. Charles Theatre. And Snoozer could play, you know, play without, play with his fingers on the, on the, on the frets, you see. Without, without stroking the strings in some of the passages, you see. And so I said, Snoozer, I want you to shake hands with Mr. Whiteman. He says, glad to know you Mr. Whiteman with that, with that head to one side, you know. And he kept on playing. And Paul, Paul caught it that quick and got a big bang out of it. And he said, wait a minute, wait a minute, keep on playing, I'll be right back, see. Keep on playing, I'll be right back. And he went to get Pinkertore, see. And he brought Mike over there and he says, Mike, I want you to meet Snoozer Quinn. And he says, glad to know you Mr. Pinkertore. And he kept on playing, you see. Shaking hands with Pinkertore and he was still playing. Well that was brand new to Paul, see. And man, he was, he said, keep on, keep on. And he went and got this piano player, wonderful person. Roy Boygie. Roy Boygie, yeah, yeah. And Harry McDonald and all that bunch of around Snoozer. Well I'll tell you what actually happened with Snoozer. Snoozer had to come home. Snoozer was from a little town in Bogalusa, Louisiana. I know. You know him, huh? Well I know people from over there used to live near him. And Snoozer was, he went up there and Paul had Snoozer on party. More than he had him in the band. He'd go around with Paul and all, partying at night with Jimmy Walker and that bunch up in New York. And pretty near kill Snoozer had to come home or he'd have died. It's hard to hold the pace with some of those fellas. Oh yeah. But really, a lot of the things in the music business that I've been around, people that I've known. I've enjoyed them all. But like I say, music has been an avocation. I could always respect the... I got to playing music steady after the Depression, during the Depression. Of course we got a few mules when we were out there playing sometimes. I never shall forget we went to play the Silver Slipper in Memphis. And Eddie Miller and Badouk and Ben Pollock and Goodman and all that. Not Ben, but his brother plays bass came through.
